oil-api-draw-iran-bid.headline: API crude draw runs 87% above forecast as US-Iran deal speculation adds a geopolitical bid
oil-api-draw-iran-bid.body_md:
American Petroleum Institute data released Tuesday showed US crude stockpiles fell by 6.750 million barrels in the latest week — nearly double the consensus draw of 3.600 million barrels and 87% larger than markets had expected. If confirmed by the Energy Information Administration on Wednesday, it would mark the sixth consecutive weekly drawdown in US commercial crude inventories, a string of declines that increasingly suggests either demand is running hotter than assumed or domestic supply constraints are tighter than the models allowed.

WTI futures settled near $94 a barrel on Tuesday, up roughly 1.7% on the session. Brent closed around $96, holding gains from a third straight positive session. Both benchmarks have been whipsawed since the Iran conflict began in early 2026 — Brent hit nearly $120 a barrel at its peak — and have since retreated as ceasefire diplomacy advanced, only to swing on each fresh headline out of the negotiating rooms.

The inventory beat adds a clean fundamental argument to a market that has been running almost entirely on geopolitical noise. A draw that large, sustained over six weeks, points to real-side tightness: refiners are running product through the system at a pace that outstrips replenishment. With the Strait of Hormuz still operating at reduced commercial capacity, domestic stocks are absorbing pressure that would ordinarily be shared with imported supply.

## The Strait Factor

The geopolitical overlay is doing work that the fundamentals alone would not justify. More than 14 million barrels per day of Gulf crude remain effectively shut in while peace talks between Washington and Tehran drag across their core disagreements — uranium enrichment limits, sanctions sequencing, verification protocols. President Trump said this week that a memorandum of understanding to reopen the Strait "could happen over the next week," a timeline Iranian officials have not confirmed and which their state media greeted with headlines designed to suggest the gap remains wide.

Traders are pricing that uncertainty in both directions. A deal that reopens the Strait would release an estimated 100 million barrels of stranded tanker cargo onto a market already bidding up the risk premium, a potential price shock downward. Oxford Economics analyst Bridget Payne offered the counter-scenario: if the closure extends into the late summer, OECD commercial stocks could reach a critical threshold by mid-September, "triggering a price spike towards $150 per barrel."

Goldman Sachs noted that oil market positioning is "significantly more limited than at the start" of the conflict, a sign that speculative money has stepped back from a trade where the range of outcomes remains unusually wide. That positioning restraint means that when the resolution — in either direction — comes, the move in futures could be larger than the headline number implies.

The EIA's official inventory count, due Wednesday morning, will either validate or trim Tuesday's API figure. The direction of the revision matters less than the cumulative trend: six draws in a row is a meaningful signal that the market's supply-demand balance, even without the Strait fully open, is tighter than consensus assumed heading into summer driving season. The next hard catalyst is the next round of US-Iran talks, which negotiators from both sides have indicated could resume before month-end.

bp-north-sea-exit-labour-tax.headline: BP weighs full North Sea exit as Labour's windfall tax makes the economics unworkable
bp-north-sea-exit-labour-tax.body_md:
BP has been hunting for the door to the UK North Sea for the better part of a year. Late last month, it looked like it had found one. Talks with Ithaca Energy over a package of North Sea assets valued at close to £2 billion reached an advanced stage before collapsing — a breakdown that leaves BP with a thinning list of options and a tax liability that is not getting smaller.

## The deal that didn't close

The assets on the table were never named publicly, but BP's North Sea portfolio is a matter of record: a 45% stake in the Clair field — the largest oilfield on the UK Continental Shelf, lying 75 kilometres west of Shetland — plus the Eastern Trough Area Project hub in the central North Sea, and a collection of associated interests. Together they produce roughly 120,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, about 5% of BP's 2.3 million barrel global daily output.

![BP Clair Ridge hull, west of Shetland — BP's 45% stake in the Clair field was among the assets in play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/BP_Clair_Ridge.JPG)

Ithaca was the natural buyer. The Aberdeen-based company is one of the largest independent North Sea operators, a FTSE 250 constituent majority-owned by Israel's Delek Group, and already a joint operator with BP on the Vorlich oilfield. The commercial logic was tidy; the negotiating positions were not.

The talks broke down over decommissioning liabilities, according to people familiar with the discussions. Late-life North Sea fields carry end-of-life commitments — plugging wells, removing platforms, restoring seabed — that run into hundreds of millions of pounds. Under UK law those liabilities cannot be abandoned; they transfer with the asset. The tax-relief structure for decommissioning costs gives both parties strong incentives to fight over the allocation, and when that allocation is unresolved the effective price of the field becomes undefined. Valuation gaps that appear bridgeable on headline numbers become unbridgeable once the decommissioning overhang is priced in. That appears to be what happened.

BP confirmed it is still exploring a transaction, leaving open the possibility of a revised deal with a different counterparty or a restructured terms package. It declined to comment on the specifics of the Ithaca discussions.

## A 78% rate that reshapes what any asset is worth

![A North Sea drilling platform — the basin's effective tax rate now stands at 78%, compressing returns for operators and buyers alike](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fa/Oil_platform_in_the_North_Sea.jpg)

The collapsed talks cannot be read in isolation from the fiscal backdrop. When the UK Labour government raised and extended the Energy Profits Levy in late 2024, the effective marginal tax rate on North Sea production climbed to 78% — a composite of 30% corporation tax, a 10% supplementary charge, and a 38% EPL surcharge — with the levy's sunset date extended to March 2030. BP quantified the incremental cost to its business at £539 million in its 2025 annual report.

That rate restructures the economics on both sides of any transaction. For a seller, high taxation compresses the post-tax cash flows that determine what an asset is worth on a discounted basis. For a buyer, the arithmetic is identical in reverse: paying close to £2 billion for a basin where 78 pence of every marginal pound flows to the Exchequer is a categorically different proposition from the same asset at a 40% rate. Decommissioning liabilities, discounted at a lower post-tax cost of capital, loom correspondingly larger. The result is a structural gap between what sellers need and what buyers can justify — and it is widening, not narrowing.

The broader pattern reflects this. Chevron and ConocoPhillips have trimmed North Sea exposure in recent years. UK Continental Shelf production today runs at roughly 20% of its year-2000 peak. A licensing moratorium on new exploration, which took effect in November 2025, has stripped out the upside optionality that once compensated buyers for accepting mature-field risk. What remains is a basin offering declining output, a decommissioning liability curve stretching decades forward, and a tax structure that limits the return on capital for anyone who stays.

## A $20 billion target and a shrinking runway

BP's new chief executive, Meg O'Neill — who replaced Murray Auchincloss in April following pressure from activist hedge fund Elliott Management — has committed to $20 billion in asset sales by end-2027 against $27 billion in net debt. The North Sea was supposed to contribute meaningfully to that figure. The failed Ithaca talks set the timetable back.

A full exit from the North Sea — where BP has operated continuously for more than 60 years — remains under active internal review, according to people with knowledge of the process. Scottish First Minister John Swinney has said he is "very concerned" by the reports. The political response has been predictable; the commercial response has not yet materialised.

The government's position has softened at the margins. Chancellor Rachel Reeves has signalled the Energy Profits Levy could be wound down by 2027, and UK officials have held bilateral discussions with North Sea producers on the levy's future. Whether that timetable is short enough to close the valuation gap on a £2 billion deal — and to do so before BP's divestiture deadline tightens — is the question the next few quarters will answer. For a prospective buyer like Ithaca, the uncertainty itself may be reason enough to wait for clearer terms from government before revisiting the table.

marvell-amd-broadcom-chip-sector-ai.headline: Jensen Huang puts Marvell in the trillion-dollar club as Barclays reframes the AI trade around CPUs
marvell-amd-broadcom-chip-sector-ai.body_md:
Marvell Technology shares closed at an all-time high on Tuesday — the company's best trading session since listing — after Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang turned a product stage in Taipei into something closer to a market event. The gap between the two companies' sizes, Huang implied, is temporary.

"The next trillion dollar company, ladies and gentlemen," Huang told the Computex audience on Monday, gesturing toward Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy beside him on stage. The remark circulated quickly. By Tuesday's close, Marvell had gained 32.52% — a record single-day move — lifting its market capitalisation from roughly $191 billion to approximately $234 billion. Reaching $1 trillion from that base would require something close to a fourfold increase. Markets appeared content to price the direction, not the distance.

What makes the moment worth examining past the headline figure is its source. Huang runs Nvidia, the company that has defined and largely captured the GPU infrastructure trade for three years. That he would publicly anoint a networking and connectivity chip maker as the sector's next landmark is a claim about which layer of the stack he believes remains undervalued.

Huang's reasoning, delivered at Computex, centres on topology. "When you take a computing problem, and you disaggregate it into a lot of parts, and you distribute it across the entire data center, what's necessary is connectivity," he said. Marvell builds the custom ASICs and networking silicon that stitch data-centre fabric together — the circulatory system for AI workloads distributed across thousands of nodes. If compute continues to scale out horizontally, that market grows with it.

![Marvell Technology's Santa Clara, California headquarters](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b2/Marvell_Santa_Clara_May_2011.jpg)
*Marvell Technology's Santa Clara campus. The company's connectivity chips are central to the case Huang made from the COMPUTEX stage.*

## The CPU thread Barclays is pulling

The endorsement arrived in the same week Tom O'Malley, Barclays' semiconductor analyst, raised his price target on Advanced Micro Devices to $665 from $500 — maintaining an Overweight rating — and argued that the AI hardware trade has been defined too narrowly for two years running.

O'Malley's thesis: the infrastructure cycle is broadening. The first phase was almost exclusively about GPUs; Nvidia dominated that conversation and most of Wall Street followed it there. But as AI workloads mature from model training toward inference and, more recently, agentic applications that run multi-step tasks continuously, the relationship between CPUs and GPUs is shifting. CPU-to-GPU ratios are tightening — meaning demand for high-performance processors beyond the GPU is rising as a share of the total compute stack.

AMD's own management provided some grounding. On the Q1 2026 earnings call, CEO Lisa Su said the company was "seeing strong momentum as inferencing and agentic AI drive increasing demand for high-performance CPUs and accelerators." That is not a hedged comment — it names the specific workload category pulling CPU demand higher.

For institutional investors who have been concentrated in GPU suppliers and light on the broader silicon infrastructure, the Barclays call and the Marvell rally appearing in the same week point toward the same conclusion: the AI infrastructure trade has a second act, and it does not belong exclusively to Nvidia.

## Broadcom and the quarterly test

The third thread — and the one with the shortest fuse — sits at Broadcom. The company reports fiscal second-quarter results on June 3, with consensus revenue at $22.1 billion, up 47% from a year earlier. AI chip revenue is expected to reach $10.7 billion for the quarter, roughly 140% higher year-on-year.

Jay Woods, chief global strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, put the stock's position plainly ahead of the print: Broadcom "may as well be" a member of the Magnificent Seven, given its trillion-dollar valuation and index weighting. The stock entered the week at $477.74, up nearly 39% year to date, with JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Susquehanna and UBS all clustered near a $500 price target.

The earnings print matters beyond one company's quarterly figures. Broadcom provides custom silicon and networking infrastructure to the AI clusters of Google, Amazon, Meta and others. If its numbers corroborate what Huang described from the Computex stage — disaggregated compute at scale, connectivity as the binding constraint — it cements what is beginning to look like a sector-wide upgrade cycle for chip infrastructure, not just for GPU suppliers.

If the numbers disappoint, the logic that is currently levitating Marvell and AMD alongside Broadcom gets harder to sustain at current valuations. That is the risk embedded quietly in a cluster of sell-side price targets all sitting just above the current share price.

Broadcom's Q2 figures and forward guidance land after the US close on June 3. For AMD, the next concrete data point is a potential custom-silicon roadmap update at a summer analyst event — the catalyst that would give O'Malley's CPU thesis specific product numbers rather than a directional argument. For Marvell, the question is whether Huang's COMPUTEX endorsement translates into disclosed design wins, or remains, for now, a conviction call from a well-placed peer.

sp500-winning-streak-1995.headline: S&P 500 chases a nine-day winning streak not seen since 1995
sp500-winning-streak-1995.body_md:
The S&P 500 closed Tuesday at 7,612, logging its ninth consecutive daily gain — and positioning itself, on Wednesday, for a milestone not seen since September 1995. Only eight times in 55 years of market data has the index extended a daily run to ten sessions. None of those came after 2001.

A nine-day streak is uncommon but not unprecedented; this one is the seventeenth of its kind since 1970, with May 2025 still fresh in the record books. It is the tenth day that represents historically thin air — and that is the threshold the market is now chasing.

## What the data say

The forward-return record after ten-day streaks is, in a word, unimpressive. Across eight prior instances, average returns lagged the market's baseline by a margin that widened the further out the measurement went. One month later, the index underperformed its historical average by 0.28 percentage points — a number small enough to dismiss. Six months later, the gap was 5.2 points, with the S&P 500 averaging a return of negative 0.70% against a historical norm of 4.5%. Twelve months out, the average gain was 2.14%, compared to the long-run expectation of roughly 9%.

Win rates confirmed the drag. The index closed higher six months after a ten-day streak in only four of eight cases — a coin flip. That figure is meaningfully below the market's unconditional hit rate over comparable periods.

The caveat is the sample. Eight data points, spread across decades and macro regimes, make clean statistical conclusions difficult. September 1995 was followed by a 16% advance over the next twelve months, as the early phase of the technology supercycle overwhelmed any mean-reversion impulse. October 1989 worked the other direction: approximately 15% losses over the same window, amplified by credit stress and the brief but sharp October mini-crash. The dispersion between those two endpoints should give anyone building a contrarian trade around streak length reason to pause.

## The rally's foundations

The run that brought the index to this point rests on two pillars: AI-driven chip demand and an earnings season that has outpaced even elevated expectations. Roughly 85% of S&P 500 companies have beaten estimates this quarter, with an average positive surprise approaching 17% — more than double the long-run average. Semiconductor names have been the sharpest contributors, a theme echoed in the week's broader chip-sector moves.

Valuation has tracked the price gains. The index trades near 21.2 times forward earnings, above historical averages but not wildly so given the earnings acceleration. The complication is the inflation backdrop: April CPI came in at 3.8%, well above target, and the Federal Reserve has held rates rather than cut. That leaves the real yield environment as a latent weight on multiples, particularly if the summer data prints surprised on the upside.

## What to watch

If Wednesday's session produces another positive close, the index will have completed a streak that, by the historical record, preceded below-average returns in five of eight subsequent six-month windows. Whether this instance resembles 1995 or 1989 will depend less on streak mechanics than on what inflation does next. The June CPI print, due in the second week of the month, is the most immediate variable: a reading that sustains or exceeds 3.8% would test whether current valuations can hold without a rate-cut catalyst.

warsh-fed-project-2025-advisers.headline: Warsh installs Project 2025 veterans at the Fed, mapping the administration's monetary direction
warsh-fed-project-2025-advisers.body_md:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh made his first staff additions to the central bank on June 2, choosing two conservative policy veterans as temporary contractors for policy analysis and planning — a choice that maps the intellectual orbit in which his chairmanship intends to operate.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the appointments. Paul Winfree, president of the Economic Policy Innovation Center, and Daniel Heil, a policy fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution, will join as contractors. Warsh has known both men for years, having worked with them on research and writing projects. Neither appointment has been made permanent.

## Two Contractors, One Telling Signal

![Paul Winfree, then serving as Deputy Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy, 2017](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f4/20170615-OSEC-LSC-0363_%2834490729374%29.jpg)

Winfree is a veteran of the first Trump White House, where he served as Deputy Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy and co-authored the administration's inaugural budget proposal alongside then-OMB Director Mick Mulvaney. He went on to chair the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board and most recently founded the Economic Policy Innovation Center, a pro-Trump think tank that has concentrated on monetary and fiscal reform. He holds a PhD in economics from Queen's University Belfast.

Heil built his career on the federal budget and antipoverty programs, advising Jeb Bush's 2016 presidential campaign on tax policy before settling in at the Hoover Institution, where his recent work has examined federal healthcare costs and Social Security reform.

The temporary nature of both positions leaves room for interpretation — Warsh has said he has not decided whether to make them permanent. But the pairing signals something about scope. Heil's expertise sits largely outside the Fed's traditional remit of monetary policy and bank supervision; his appointment suggests Warsh is building something broader than a conventional policy shop.

## The Blueprint on the Table

Winfree's hiring carries ideological weight that goes beyond résumé. He is the named author of the Federal Reserve chapter in the Heritage Foundation's ninth edition of *Mandate for Leadership* — the policy compendium that provided the framework for Project 2025. That chapter canvassed a range of structural reforms, most notably a proposal to replace the Fed's dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability with a narrower directive to "protect the dollar and restrain inflation." It also addressed the Fed's communication practices, its balance sheet, and the broader question of central bank independence.

The chapter explored terrain that goes further than anything Warsh has publicly endorsed. But its author is now inside the building.

## Alignment, Distance, and What to Watch

Warsh has been careful to mark distance from the most aggressive Project 2025 proposals. At his swearing-in ceremony on May 22, he sent a memo to more than 20,000 Fed employees pledging to respect "the best of the Fed's traditions, while also looking for change." He has spoken in measured terms about honoring both sides of the dual mandate — a direct public departure from Winfree's Project 2025 position.

His stated reform priorities cluster around structural matters: reducing the Fed's $6.7 trillion balance sheet, scaling back highly specific forward guidance, and reconsidering how the central bank measures inflation. Warsh has for years been a vocal critic of large-scale asset purchases — he has called them "reverse Robin Hood," arguing they support financial asset prices while doing comparatively little for the broader economy and widening wealth gaps.

Still, the gap between stated positions and staffing choices invites scrutiny. The Senate confirmed Warsh 54-45 in May — the most contested confirmation in the Fed's history — in part because of concerns about whether he would use the chair to advance the administration's monetary preferences. Hiring the architect of Project 2025's Fed overhaul as a first act does not simplify that question.

The Fed's first rate-setting meeting under Warsh's chairmanship is scheduled for June 16-17. Whether Winfree and Heil transition from contractors to permanent staff will be an early and concrete signal of how deep the Project 2025 influence is intended to run. A Supreme Court ruling on presidential removal powers — which could affect the legal standing of Fed board members — remains pending and adds a further layer of institutional uncertainty. Investors watching rate expectations should track both.

fluence-nvidia-siemens-grid-storage.headline: Fluence Energy surges as Nvidia and Siemens back grid-storage blueprints for AI data centres
fluence-nvidia-siemens-grid-storage.body_md:
On Monday afternoon, shares of Fluence Energy climbed a further 5.1%, the second consecutive session of notable gains after the electricity storage specialist announced a three-way collaboration with Siemens and Nvidia to design the power infrastructure for next-generation artificial intelligence data centres. The stock has now risen more than 47% across three trading days — a cumulative move that reflects something beyond ordinary market noise: two of the world's most formidable industrial names have put a formal stamp on grid-scale battery storage as non-negotiable infrastructure for the AI era.

## Blueprint for a 136-Megawatt Future

The centrepiece of the announcement is a reference architecture — an engineering blueprint — developed by Siemens for data centres built around Nvidia's DSX Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, the company's next-generation rack-scale AI supercomputer. Fluence's SmartStack battery system is the sole battery energy storage component specified throughout the design.

The blueprint covers the complete electrical pathway for a 136-megawatt facility — 100 megawatts of IT load — from a 34.5-kilovolt utility connection through medium- and low-voltage distribution, all the way to individual rack interfaces. It is built to Tier III concurrent maintainability standards, meaning components can be serviced without taking the facility offline. Prefabricated power skids from Siemens shorten commissioning time, and a modular architecture allows capacity to scale from tens of megawatts to hundreds without a wholesale redesign.

One specification stands out: the design calls for two to three hours of battery discharge capacity. Most analysts modelling battery storage in data centres had assumed roughly one hour. That gap implies more hardware per facility and more revenue per deployment for Fluence — a detail the market has clearly noticed.

## What SmartStack Actually Does in an AI Factory

![Data-centre backup batteries: the new Siemens design specifies 2–3 hours of storage capacity, higher than prior analyst assumptions](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Datacenter_Backup_Batteries.jpg/800px-Datacenter_Backup_Batteries.jpg)

Battery storage in data centres is often described in vague terms. In Siemens' design, SmartStack has specific, named functions.

The first is ride-through: when the utility grid experiences voltage or frequency fluctuations — increasingly common as grids absorb more variable renewable generation — the batteries maintain steady power delivery to computing equipment. The second is black start: in a full outage, the system can restart operations without waiting for grid restoration. The third is load smoothing: AI workloads consume electricity unevenly, with sharp spikes during model inference, and batteries absorb those surges so the facility does not hammer the grid or overload transformers.

"By providing essential capabilities like voltage and frequency ride-through, black start, grid demand response, and AI load smoothing," said Jeff Monday, Fluence's chief growth officer, the SmartStack technology addresses "one of the most operationally challenging aspects of running dense AI computing infrastructure at scale."

Fluence's position in the Nvidia ecosystem is unusually concentrated: the company is the only named battery energy storage provider across all seven infrastructure OEM configurations in Nvidia's partner network. That exclusivity — even if the reference architecture is not a binding purchase agreement — gives Fluence a significant first-mover position in specification discussions with hyperscalers and co-location providers who use these blueprints as starting points for facility design.

## The Bottleneck Has Shifted

![A grid-scale battery installation: the type of infrastructure Siemens' reference architecture calls for at data-centre scale](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Invenergy_Beech_Ridge_Energy_Storage_System.jpg/1200px-Invenergy_Beech_Ridge_Energy_Storage_System.jpg)

Until recently, the limiting factor in building out AI data centres was chips: supply was constrained and delivery times stretched. That pressure has eased. The constraint is now, in a growing number of markets, power.

In July 2024, a single voltage fluctuation in Northern Virginia disconnected sixty data centres simultaneously — creating a 1,500-megawatt power surplus in an instant and illustrating in stark terms how poorly the grid handles concentrated, spiky AI demand. Gartner has estimated that power shortages will restrict 40% of AI data centres by 2027. Site selection for new facilities has already shifted from questions of fibre access and latency to a search for available megawatts.

Fluence sits at that intersection. The company ended its most recent half-year with $5.6 billion in contracted backlog and reported order intake of $2 billion for H1 FY2026, double the comparable period in 2025. It has signed master supply agreements with two major hyperscalers and expects its first order from those agreements to land during the current quarter. Full-year revenue guidance stands at $3.2 to $3.4 billion.

The Siemens relationship is not new — the German industrial conglomerate co-founded Fluence as a joint venture with AES Corporation in 2018, before Fluence listed publicly in 2021. What is new is the scale and specificity of the commercial alignment. The reference architecture formalises Fluence as the natural battery choice for anyone adopting Siemens' power design — a distribution channel that Fluence's sales team could not replicate on its own.

For Siemens AG itself, the architecture represents an extension into a data-centre market that has been reshaping capital spending across the industrial sector. The company's stock has posted gains across the past day, week, month, and three-month periods, a run that reflects broadening investor recognition of Siemens' exposure to grid infrastructure demand.

## The Market's Verdict — and Its Caveats

The initial market reaction was dramatic. Fluence shares surged approximately 44% on the first day of trading after the announcement, jumping to roughly $27.15. The stock remains about 12% below its February 2026 peak of $32.23 — a reminder of how far it fell before this week's recovery.

Analysts have been more measured. The consensus Wall Street rating on FLNC is Hold, with a mean price target of $18.47 — implying significant downside from current levels if the partnership excitement fades without translating to revenue. The critical caveat: a reference architecture is a blueprint, not an order book. Hyperscalers could adopt Siemens' electrical systems and source batteries from a competitor. Nothing legally compels them to use SmartStack.

Fluence's most recent quarterly results offer mixed evidence on execution. Q2 revenue came in at $465 million against a consensus expectation of $622 million, with supply-chain delays and commodity volatility cited. Insider selling has also drawn scrutiny: management and early investors are reported to have sold more than $400 million of stock over a recent three-month period — a figure that sits uneasily alongside the bullish messaging of the current announcement cycle.

The clearest near-term test is whether Fluence converts one of its two hyperscaler master supply agreements into an actual purchase order this quarter — the company's own guidance says that is expected. If that order materialises, it begins to close the gap between blueprint-level validation and revenue-level reality. Until then, the partnership confirms that the world's largest chip company and one of its most powerful industrial groups have decided battery storage belongs at the centre of every serious AI data centre design — a bet on infrastructure that would have seemed premature two years ago.

goldman-solomon-ai-greed.headline: Goldman's Solomon calls AI funding a 'greed'-driven frenzy
goldman-solomon-ai-greed.body_md:
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said on Monday that investors have tilted decisively into "greed" mode, a characterisation he offered as markets prepare to absorb the largest fundraising wave in AI history — and one that carried an implicit note of caution from the bank advising many of those deals.

Speaking to CNBC's Leslie Picker on June 2, Solomon was blunt: "We are definitely in a moment where there's more greed than there is fear." The remark draws on the classic Wall Street sentiment spectrum — fear and greed as the two poles between which rational pricing gives way to instinct — and came as three of the largest anticipated public offerings in market history edge toward their roadshows.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX are each preparing listings at valuations that, combined, approach $3.6 trillion — roughly the GDP of France. Anthropic just closed a $65 billion Series H at a post-money valuation of $965 billion; OpenAI is generating $25 billion in annualised revenue at an $852 billion private valuation; SpaceX is eyeing a raise of up to $75 billion as early as next week at a $1.8-2 trillion price tag. Goldman analysts project total 2026 IPO proceeds could reach $160 billion, roughly four times last year's figure.

Solomon's evidence that markets can absorb this: Alphabet's $80 billion follow-on equity offering — the largest of its kind on record — which he called his "first actual concrete data point" for what public investors are willing to commit at scale. "There's plenty of liquidity in the system if the world continues to remain as optimistic," he said.

## Exuberance with a caveat

Solomon did not predict a crash. He acknowledged the cycle explicitly: "Greed can turn into fear very quickly, but that doesn't mean it will." And he offered a view that may unsettle the more bearish camp: "Exuberance can go on for big periods of time. There's a good chance that we're earlier in the cycle than later."

His advice to capital-hungry companies was equally direct: "When capital's available, if you're capital consumptive and it's available, take the capital."

For traders, the significance lies not in what Solomon said but who is saying it. Goldman is the underwriter and adviser of choice across this deal pipeline. The bank profits when equity is issued, and its CEO has now publicly named the mood as "greed" — language that typically precedes a recalibration, even if timing is anyone's guess. Short seller Michael Burry, in a May 2026 Substack post, drew comparisons to the final months of the 1999-2000 bubble. Morgan Stanley analysts have pushed back, arguing bubble fears are "misplaced" given that today's AI leaders generate real revenue and margins their dot-com predecessors did not.

The immediate test is the SpaceX roadshow, expected to begin as early as June 4. If that $75 billion raise is absorbed without visible stress — and if OpenAI follows in September as signalled — Solomon's earlier-in-the-cycle thesis gets a hard data point. If demand frays under the weight of three concurrent trillion-dollar offerings, the greed-to-fear turn he flagged could arrive faster than the current sentiment would suggest.

hsbc-valuation-69-pct-run.headline: HSBC's 69% annual run leaves valuation with little room for disappointment
hsbc-valuation-69-pct-run.body_md:
HSBC Holdings shares have climbed 68.7% over the past twelve months, carrying the stock from the mid-800p range to around 1,400p on the London Stock Exchange. The recovery has been real and, in operational terms, earned. The harder question — the one that matters for anyone assessing the stock today — is whether that recovery is now fully priced.

At roughly 1,399p as of the close on 2 June, HSBC trades on a trailing P/E of 15.2x. That compares unfavourably with European banking peers, whose average multiple sits at 11.4x, and with a broader global bank cross-section averaging 10.8x. Simply Wall St places a fair P/E for HSBC at 10.8x — implying the market has already awarded a premium the bank has not yet fully grown into. The most-followed narrative valuation — a discounted cash flow approach using an 8.29% discount rate applied to projected earnings — arrives at an intrinsic value of £13.67. The current price of £13.99 sits barely 3% above that figure. For a stock that has almost doubled in twelve months, the margin for error is thin.

## Two models, one uncomfortable message

The valuation picture is not straightforward. The P/E lens and the excess-returns model deliver sharply different verdicts. The latter capitalises HSBC's return on equity above its cost of capital and calculates intrinsic value at £21.66 — implying the stock is 35% undervalued. That reading is anchored to an average ROE of 15.93%, which Q1 2026's 18.7% return on tangible equity helps to support. In a rising-earnings environment, the excess-returns model earns its optimism. In a mean-reversion scenario, it flatters.

The composite score tells a colder story: Simply Wall St rates HSBC 2 out of 6 on its valuation checklist. Analysts are less pessimistic — consensus sits at Moderate Buy, with average 12-month targets clustering between 1,375p and 1,467p — but that implies perhaps 5% upside at the last close, which is not the kind of cushion that follows naturally from a 69% annual run.

The operational foundation beneath the share price is not contested. The strategic pivot from underperforming European and US businesses toward Asia and the Middle East is producing results. Total wealth balances reached $1.57 trillion in Q1 2026, up 12% year-on-year; Asian client assets grew 14% to $1.07 trillion, and net new money inflows accelerated to $39bn in the quarter from $23bn a year earlier. Net interest margins held at 1.60%, broadly flat in a choppy rate environment. The difficulty is that the market knows all of this. A P/E of 15x against peers at 11x is not a sceptical market awaiting evidence; it is a market that has priced the transformation in.

Any shortfall — prolonged stress in Hong Kong commercial real estate, an unexpected rate cut compressing Asian margins, or a stumble in wealth inflows — lands against a multiple that provides no buffer. The bank's half-year results, due in August, will be the first real test of whether Q1's 18.7% RoTE is the new baseline or a high-water mark. The direction of short rates across Asia, and any update on Hong Kong property exposure, will do more to settle the valuation debate than any model.

new-york-data-centre-moratorium.headline: New York lawmakers move to impose a one-year data centre construction freeze
new-york-data-centre-moratorium.body_md:
New York's state legislature is on course to pass a one-year moratorium on new large-scale data centre approvals — a move that would make it the first state in the country to impose such a statewide ban.

Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie said this week that lawmakers "intend to pass it," referring to legislation (S10642/A11560) co-sponsored by state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Didi Barrett. The chamber was expected to vote before the legislative session closes on Friday. The bill cleared its initial hurdles after lawmakers trimmed what had originally been proposed as a three-year freeze down to one year — enough to secure the votes, short enough to survive the political room.

## The math behind the freeze

The immediate driver is electricity demand, and the numbers are striking. The New York Independent System Operator currently has 48 new large-load projects in its interconnection queue, totalling more than 11 gigawatts. Data centres account for the bulk of that load. Projected data-centre electricity demand alone could reach 7,000 megawatts by 2030 — enough to power seven million homes. Set against that, electricity rates in New York rose 13 percent in 2025, with data centre construction cited as a contributing factor.

The NYISO's own vice president acknowledged the pressure plainly: "It's a concern because we're not adding commensurate supply to meet that forecasted demand."

The bill targets facilities designed to draw at least 20 megawatts, which captures hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure projects rather than ordinary commercial server rooms. During the one-year pause, the Department of Environmental Conservation would produce a generic environmental impact statement, and the Public Service Commission would assess how data-centre loads affect rates for residential and commercial ratepayers.

## A governor with reservations

Governor Kathy Hochul has not committed to signing the bill and has positioned herself as sceptical of statewide action. Her view is that data-centre siting is "a local decision for municipalities" and a matter of land-use law rather than state regulation. She has separately floated a different approach: require large facilities to either generate their own power or pay a premium that shields residential customers from cost pass-through.

Without her signature, the bill dies. With it, New York becomes the first state to formally pause AI-era data centre expansion on grid-capacity grounds — a precedent that would invite litigation and legislative mimicry in roughly equal measure.

Cloud operators with live construction programmes in Virginia, Texas, and the southeast have limited immediate exposure to a New York pause. The longer-run signal is harder to ignore: if electricity grids are treated as a rationed public resource, permitting timelines for new AI infrastructure will lengthen materially in states that follow New York's lead.

Hochul has offered no public timeline for her decision. The session closes Friday.

loreal-analyst-fair-value.headline: L'Oréal's analyst fair value edges up €2.27—a shift that matters more at the margin than in aggregate
loreal-analyst-fair-value.body_md:
L'Oréal's analyst fair value number, as computed by Simply Wall St's discounted cash flow model, has moved to €408.42 from €406.15 — a gain of €2.27, or roughly half a per cent. For most portfolio constructions, that decimal shift sits below the noise floor. For traders running tight entry-and-exit disciplines, a drifting fair-value peg is still worth logging, even if it changes nothing about the underlying thesis.

The source of the revision is model recalibration, not a fresh conviction call. The inputs barely moved: revenue growth assumptions edged from 5.37 per cent to 5.36 per cent (actually fractionally lower), net profit margins crept from 16.08 to 16.10 per cent, the forward P/E multiple stepped up from 31.99x to 32.16x, and the discount rate shifted from 6.78 to 6.81 per cent. In aggregate these adjustments are rounding — what the model changed was how those small inputs compound through the algebra, not the shape of L'Oréal's business.

## Where the real disagreement lives

The gap between the Simply Wall St. DCF and the broader analyst community is where the story gets more interesting. Berenberg recently upgraded L'Oréal to Buy with a €435 target, up sharply from €374, citing what the bank called "an inflection point in the company's growth profile." Its thesis: L'Oréal is returning to its historical organic growth rate and the market has not fully priced that back in. HSBC shares the view at a €437 Buy target. Both upgrades followed a first-quarter 2026 print in which like-for-like revenues grew 7.6 per cent — a beat on consensus — and L'Oréal formally closed its €4 billion Kering Beauté acquisition at the end of March.

Against that, Morgan Stanley maintained Equal Weight at €370, a target more than 9 per cent below the bullish cluster. That spread is unusually wide for a stock this well-covered, and it points at a genuine dispute: does the strong Q1 represent a durable return to form, or a cyclical uptick ahead of tighter demand in 2027? The Simply Wall St. DCF, with its sub-1 per cent nudge, does not adjudicate that question. Its 5.36 per cent annual revenue growth assumption sits neatly between the bulls and the bears without endorsing either — which is both the strength and the limitation of a mechanistic model.

Recent price action suggests the market has aligned itself closer to the Berenberg camp. A 7.2 per cent monthly gain following the Q1 beat is not the behaviour of a stock where investors doubt the growth story. Whether that momentum sustains depends on whether L'Oréal can absorb the Kering Beauté integration cleanly and on demand conditions in the group's emerging-market expansion zones — Mexico, Brazil, India, and Thailand — as the second half approaches.

The half-year results will be the clearest next read: they will carry the first full quarter of Kering Beauté on the books, alongside a Q2 demand signal from China and selective consumer markets. Until then, €408 is less a forecast than a placeholder — a model that has been nudged, not remade.
